Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette: At thirty-eight, Elias, an American of Lebanese descent, was navigating a fractured city as a relief coordinator. He remembers the acrid smoke of burning timber and fuel wrapping around the checkpoint where his convoy halted. The air was thick with ash, the radio static of military patrols cutting through the usual chaos of the district. He never had the chance to piece the days together afterward. What remained were disconnected fragments: a collapsed awning, the sudden hush of a street just before the ground shook, a soldier's urgent gestures he could not quite read. When those pieces surface now, the terror hits him with the same force as it did then, flooding his chest and throat until he has to step away and ground himself in the room. Over the years, as he transitioned into American politics, the old patterns settled into his routine. He kept his posture rigid, treating emotional restraint as a necessary discipline. He would pivot to policy briefs, focus on constituency data, or volunteer for evening hearings to occupy every hour without leaving room for stillness. The quiet in his home grew heavy. An uncharacteristic pause in a conversation or an empty hallway made him certain that something dangerous was about to happen. Alongside this, he began walking the perimeter of his house, testing each deadbolt, watching every window until his shoulders ached, convinced that security was measured in clicks and latches. His work as a politician became the landscape where these habits played out. In campaign offices and legislative hearings, he found himself constantly scanning the room, tracking sightlines and reading shifts in tension the way he once read a checkpoint. When donors or aides drifted into talk of military strategy or troop deployments, his attention narrowed; the subject suddenly felt too close to the ground he had tried to leave behind. Strangers approaching his table to ask questions or offer condolences triggered a familiar rush of vigilance. He would answer politely, but his focus never fully landed, always partitioned toward the exits and the faint drafts that carried the ghost of smoke. The overwork piled up. He missed family gatherings, let his house settle into disarray, and kept his schedule packed to the brim. His former wife had moved on long ago, their shared life gradually replaced by the quiet distance of parallel routines. Now, at sixty-four, Elias sits across from a clinician for the first time. He has come because the hearings run longer, his sleep has fractured, and he can no longer outrun the moments when a passing scent of charred wood or a sudden hush in a committee room drops him back into the wreckage. He is afraid that the ground will give out beneath him again, that the scattered pieces will keep pulling him backward. What he hopes for, quietly, is a way to stand still without bracing, to let a room be quiet without measuring its weight, and to finally rest his hands.
